processing: Finished black tea is layered with fresh jasmine blossoms so it takes up their scent, typically over several rounds with drying between them.
harvest_season: The base tea is picked in its own season; scenting with fresh flowers waits for the jasmine to bloom.
appearance_dry: Dark twisted black leaf, as with other scented black teas, sometimes with a few spent petals left in.
appearance_liquor: Clear reddish amber, typical of a Chinese black tea.
appearance_wet: Soft brown-copper leaf, with the look of the base tea rather than of the flower.
taste_profile: Expect sweet jasmine perfume on the nose over the malt and gentle cocoa of a Chinese black tea; the exact balance depends on the base and the number of scenting rounds.

brewing.notes: Generic starting point for a scented black tea, not a fixed rule. Slightly cooler water keeps the flower from going soapy against the tannin.

vintage_note: Usually sold without a vintage, as a scented tea of the current or recent year, since scenting happens once a year when the jasmine blooms. As with other scented teas, the perfume fades with time, so buy small and drink it within a year or so.
description:
Black Jasmine is what it sounds like: black tea scented with fresh jasmine flowers instead of the usual green or white base. It is a style rather than a single named tea from one place, and shops build it on different bases. Keemun from Anhui is one example.

The method is close to that of green jasmine tea, and the main difference is the base leaf. Blossoms are picked before the midday heat and laid on the tea as they open. Better lots go through several rounds.

In the cup you should get flower on the nose and black tea on the tongue. A dark base with its own malt can stand up to jasmine, but it can also fight it, and that clash is the risk with this style. Treat it gently, with water a little off the boil and steeps that are not too long.

When buying, ask what the base tea is and how many rounds of scenting it had. As with other jasmine teas, a loud perfume that vanishes after one steep suggests flavouring rather than flowers.
history: Little is documented about this style's origins. No date, place or maker can be attached to it.
